rte-balboa-sights-pacific.why: Balboa had fled his debts on Hispaniola as a stowaway and risen to lead the Spanish settlement of Santa María la Antigua del Darién. Indigenous informants told him of another sea to the south and of lands rich in gold, and he hoped a great discovery would win royal favour.
rte-balboa-sights-pacific.impact: The sighting showed that an ocean lay beyond the Americas and that Panama was a narrow crossing point. Spain later used the isthmus to move Peruvian silver towards Europe. Balboa gained little. His rival Pedrarias Dávila had him beheaded on a treason charge in 1519.

rte-magellan-enters-strait.why: The Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 left Portugal the eastern route to the Spice Islands, so Spain wanted a western one. Magellan, a Portuguese veteran of the Indies who had been refused backing at home, persuaded the young Charles I of Spain that a passage existed through South America.
rte-magellan-enters-strait.impact: The strait proved that ships could sail from the Atlantic into the Pacific. Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521, but one ship, the Victoria under Juan Sebastián Elcano, reached Spain in 1522 and completed the first circumnavigation. The strait itself long remained a difficult and little-used route.

rte-st-augustine-founded.why: Spanish treasure fleets sailed home along the Florida coast on the Gulf Stream, and a French Protestant colony planted there in 1564 threatened them. Philip II also saw the Huguenots as heretics on land that Spain claimed. Earlier Spanish attempts to settle Florida had all failed.
rte-st-augustine-founded.impact: The town became the capital of Spanish Florida and a base for missions among the Timucua and other peoples. It survived raids, including one by Francis Drake in 1586, and Spain later built the stone Castillo de San Marcos to defend it. Florida passed to the United States in 1821.

rte-hudson-new-york-bay.why: The Dutch East India Company wanted a shorter route to Asia than the long voyage round Africa. Hudson first sailed north-east towards Novaya Zemlya, but ice blocked his way. He then turned west across the Atlantic, hoping that a passage might lie through North America.
rte-hudson-new-york-bay.impact: The Dutch claim based on his voyage led to trading posts on the river and a settlement on Manhattan in the 1620s. England seized the colony in 1664 and renamed it New York. Hudson was set adrift by mutineers in 1611 in the bay named after him, and was never seen again.

rte-cook-killed-hawaii.why: Cook's third voyage had been sent to look for a Northwest Passage from the Pacific side. He reached Hawaii in 1778 and returned during the Makahiki festival, when he was received with great honour. Scholars still debate whether Hawaiians regarded him as the god Lono.
rte-cook-killed-hawaii.impact: The expedition carried on under Charles Clerke and then John Gore, reaching Britain in 1780. Cook's charts and journals guided later Pacific navigation and opened Hawaii to foreign ships, trade and disease. His reputation remains contested, celebrated as a navigator and criticised as an agent of colonisation.

rte-ponce-de-leon-florida.why: Ponce de León had been governor of Puerto Rico but lost the post in a dispute with Diego Columbus. The Crown granted him a licence to find and settle lands said to lie to the north. The story that he sought a Fountain of Youth appears only in later accounts.
rte-ponce-de-leon-florida.impact: Spanish pilots soon used the Gulf Stream to speed treasure fleets home to Europe. Ponce de León returned in 1521 to found a colony, but was wounded in a fight with the Calusa and died in Cuba. Lasting Spanish settlement in Florida came only in 1565.

rte-cartier-cross-gaspe.why: Francis I of France refused to accept that Spain and Portugal could divide the new lands between them, and he wanted a share of their wealth. He commissioned Cartier, an experienced sailor from Saint-Malo, to look for gold and a passage to Asia beyond the fishing grounds of Newfoundland.
rte-cartier-cross-gaspe.impact: Cartier returned in 1535 and sailed up the St Lawrence as far as the sites of Quebec and Montreal. His attempt at a colony in the 1540s failed, but his voyages fixed French interest on the river. Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec there in 1608.

rte-de-soto-mississippi.why: De Soto had grown rich as a captain in the conquest of Peru and hoped to find another wealthy empire. Charles V named him governor of Cuba with the right to conquer Florida, and he landed on its west coast in 1539 with several hundred men.
rte-de-soto-mississippi.impact: The survivors reached Mexico in 1543. Their accounts are the main written record of the Mississippian chiefdoms of the Southeast. The expedition's violence and, many historians think, the diseases it carried damaged those societies, and later Europeans found the region much changed.

rte-roggeveen-easter-island.why: Roggeveen sailed for the Dutch West India Company, taking up a plan his father had proposed decades earlier to find the southern continent. He was also looking for land reported by the English buccaneer Edward Davis in the eastern Pacific, which he hoped would open new trade.
rte-roggeveen-easter-island.impact: The visit lasted only days and included Dutch sailors shooting a number of islanders. It gave Europe its first description of the moai. Later contact was far more damaging. Slave raids from Peru in the 1860s and disease left only a few hundred Rapa Nui, and Chile annexed the island in 1888.

rte-la-salle-claims-louisiana.why: French traders and missionaries had pushed west from the St Lawrence to the Great Lakes, and Jolliet and Marquette had shown in 1673 that the Mississippi flowed south. La Salle, a fur trader backed by Governor Frontenac, wanted to confirm it reached the Gulf and to control its trade.
rte-la-salle-claims-louisiana.impact: La Salle returned by sea in 1684 to found a colony, but landed in Texas by mistake and was murdered by his own men in 1687. France founded New Orleans in 1718. Napoleon sold the territory to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.

rte-mendana-solomon-islands.why: Stories in Peru, some drawn from Inca tradition, told of rich islands to the west. The navigator Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa urged an expedition, and the governor of Peru gave command to his young nephew Mendaña, with orders to find the lands and convert their people.
rte-mendana-solomon-islands.impact: The Spaniards spent about six months in the islands, clashing with their inhabitants over food, and found no gold. Mendaña sailed again in 1595 but missed the Solomons and died on Santa Cruz. European contact resumed in the eighteenth century, and Britain declared a protectorate in 1893.

rte-orellana-amazon-mouth.why: Gonzalo Pizarro had set out from Quito in 1541 with a large expedition to look for cinnamon forests and the rumoured kingdom of El Dorado. In the rainforest its supplies ran out and men began to starve, so Orellana went ahead with a boat and about fifty men.
rte-orellana-amazon-mouth.impact: Friar Gaspar de Carvajal's account described large settlements along the banks, a claim long doubted but given some support by modern archaeology. Orellana died on a return expedition in 1546. Spain did little to follow up the voyage, and Portugal came to control most of the river.

rte-bering-sights-alaska.why: Peter the Great had ordered an expedition to learn whether Asia and America were joined. Bering's first voyage in 1728 passed through the strait between them without sighting America. The far larger second expedition was sent to chart Siberia's coasts and reach the American shore.
rte-bering-sights-alaska.impact: Survivors brought back sea otter pelts, and Russian hunters soon worked their way along the Aleutian Islands, often with great brutality towards the Aleut people. The naturalist Georg Steller described several animals new to science. Russia held Alaska until it sold the territory to the United States in 1867.

rte-cook-antarctic-circle.why: Cook's first voyage had shown that New Zealand was not part of a southern continent, but the wider question remained open. The Admiralty sent him back with two ships to settle it. He carried a copy of John Harrison's chronometer, which let him fix longitude accurately.
rte-cook-antarctic-circle.impact: Cook circled the globe at high southern latitudes and crossed the circle twice more, reaching about 71 degrees south in 1774. He never saw Antarctica, which was first sighted in 1820. His reports of abundant seals at South Georgia drew sealing ships into the Southern Ocean.

rte-mackenzie-reaches-pacific.why: Mackenzie worked for the North West Company, which wanted a route to the Pacific so that it could ship furs to China and cut its costs. In 1789 he had followed a great river from Great Slave Lake, hoping it led west, but it carried him to the Arctic Ocean.
rte-mackenzie-reaches-pacific.impact: His route was too difficult for trade, but his journal, published in 1801, was widely read. Thomas Jefferson is known to have read it, and it helped prompt the Lewis and Clark expedition. The crossing also supported later British claims to the Pacific coast.

rte-luther-diet-of-worms.why: Luther's Ninety-five Theses of 1517 had attacked the sale of indulgences, and his later writings rejected papal authority itself. Pope Leo X excommunicated him in January 1521. His prince, Frederick the Wise of Saxony, insisted that he be heard on German soil before any sentence was carried out.
rte-luther-diet-of-worms.impact: At the Wartburg Luther translated the New Testament into German, which spread his ideas and helped shape the written language. The edict was never properly enforced, as several princes protected the reformers. Within a decade western Christianity was dividing into rival churches.

rte-copernicus-de-revolutionibus.why: Ptolemy's system predicted planetary positions only by using complicated devices that some astronomers found unsatisfying. Copernicus, a church canon at Frombork, had circulated a sun-centred outline decades earlier but hesitated to publish. A young mathematician, Georg Joachim Rheticus, visited him and persuaded him to release the full work.
rte-copernicus-de-revolutionibus.impact: An unsigned preface added by Andreas Osiander presented the theory as a mere calculating device, which blunted early reactions. Few readers accepted a moving Earth at first. The Catholic Church placed the book on its Index in 1616 pending corrections, and it stayed there until the nineteenth century.

rte-st-bartholomews-day-massacre.why: France had fought three civil wars since 1562. Many Huguenot nobles were in Paris for the marriage of Henry of Navarre to the king's sister Margaret. A failed attempt on Coligny's life two days earlier raised fears of Protestant revenge. Who ordered the killings is still debated.
rte-st-bartholomews-day-massacre.impact: Estimates of the dead vary widely, from about five thousand to thirty thousand across France. Henry of Navarre survived by converting under pressure. Many Huguenots abandoned their faith or fled abroad, while some writers began to justify resistance to tyrannical kings. The wars continued into the 1590s.

rte-galileo-sentenced.why: In 1616 the Church had declared Copernican theory contrary to Scripture and warned Galileo not to defend it. He believed his old acquaintance Pope Urban VIII would allow a balanced discussion. But the Dialogue put the Pope's own argument into the mouth of a character called Simplicio.
rte-galileo-sentenced.impact: The Dialogue was banned, and Catholic scholars grew more cautious about astronomy. Galileo's last book, Two New Sciences, was smuggled out and printed in Leiden in 1638. In 1992 Pope John Paul II formally acknowledged that the Church had erred in the case.

rte-king-james-bible.why: At the Hampton Court Conference of 1604, Puritan leaders asked James I for a new translation. James disliked the popular Geneva Bible, whose marginal notes he thought questioned royal authority. He wanted one version, without such notes, that the whole English Church could use.
rte-king-james-bible.impact: It replaced the Geneva Bible only gradually, becoming the standard English Bible by the later seventeenth century. Much of its wording drew on William Tyndale's earlier translation. It travelled with English-speaking settlers and missionaries and remained dominant in Protestant churches until the twentieth century.

rte-act-of-supremacy.why: Henry wanted a male heir and wished to marry Anne Boleyn. Pope Clement VII was under the influence of Emperor Charles V, Catherine's nephew, and would not grant the annulment. From 1532 Thomas Cromwell steered laws through Parliament that cut off appeals and payments to Rome.
rte-act-of-supremacy.impact: Denying the royal supremacy became treason, and Thomas More and Bishop John Fisher were executed in 1535. Monastic lands passed to the Crown and then largely to the gentry. Mary I restored papal authority, but Elizabeth I's settlement of 1559 made the break permanent.

rte-edict-of-nantes.why: France had suffered a series of religious wars since 1562. When Henry inherited the throne in 1589, the Catholic League and Spain refused to accept a Protestant king. By 1598 he had defeated or bought off his opponents, and his former Huguenot allies demanded guarantees for their safety.
rte-edict-of-nantes.impact: The settlement also let the Huguenots garrison fortified towns such as La Rochelle, a privilege Cardinal Richelieu removed in the 1620s. After the revocation of 1685, some 200,000 Huguenots by common estimates fled to England, the Dutch Republic, Prussia and elsewhere, taking their skills with them.

rte-peace-of-augsburg.why: Charles V had defeated the Protestant Schmalkaldic League at Mühlberg in 1547 but could not impose a religious settlement. A revolt by the princes in 1552, backed by France, forced him to flee. Exhausted, he left the negotiations to his brother Ferdinand and soon abdicated.
rte-peace-of-augsburg.impact: The peace recognised only Catholics and Lutherans, leaving out Calvinists and Anabaptists. Subjects who rejected their ruler's faith were allowed to emigrate. Disputes over church lands and the growth of Calvinism strained the settlement, and the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 extended recognition to Calvinists.

rte-sidereus-nuncius.why: Spectacle makers in the Netherlands produced the first telescopes in 1608. Galileo, a mathematics professor at Padua, heard of the device in 1609 and built much stronger versions of his own. He rushed his findings into print within weeks to secure credit before anyone else.
rte-sidereus-nuncius.impact: Galileo named Jupiter's moons the Medicean Stars and won a post at the court of Cosimo II de' Medici in Florence. The moons showed that not everything circled the Earth. Kepler quickly endorsed the findings, and the telescope became a standard tool of astronomy.

rte-sack-of-rome.why: France and the Habsburgs had fought over Italy for decades. After Charles V captured Francis I at Pavia in 1525, Pope Clement VII joined the League of Cognac against the emperor. The imperial army in Italy marched on Rome under the Duke of Bourbon, who was killed in the assault.
rte-sack-of-rome.impact: Clement paid a large ransom and made peace, crowning Charles emperor at Bologna in 1530. With the Pope dependent on Catherine of Aragon's nephew, Henry VIII's hopes of an annulment faded. Rome's population fell sharply, and many of its artists left for other cities.

rte-council-of-trent-opens.why: Reformers had called for a general council since the early years of Luther's protest. Popes delayed, fearing a council might claim authority over them, and wars between Charles V and France caused further postponements. Trent was chosen as a city of the Empire on the Italian side of the Alps.
rte-council-of-trent-opens.impact: The council affirmed seven sacraments, the authority of tradition alongside Scripture, and the Latin Vulgate. It ordered seminaries in every diocese and required bishops to live in their sees. Its decrees, with a new catechism and missal, guided Catholic practice until the Second Vatican Council in the 1960s.

rte-vesalius-fabrica.why: Medical teaching relied on Galen, whose anatomy rested largely on dissecting animals such as apes and pigs. At Padua, Vesalius broke with custom by dissecting bodies himself while lecturing. A local judge supplied him with the corpses of executed criminals, and artists thought to be linked to Titian's workshop drew the plates.
rte-vesalius-fabrica.impact: Vesalius dedicated the book to Charles V and soon became an imperial physician. Traditionalists attacked him, but his illustrations were copied across Europe for generations. Padua remained a leading school of anatomy, and one of its later professors, Fabricius, taught William Harvey.

rte-harvey-de-motu-cordis.why: Harvey studied at Padua under Fabricius, who had described valves in the veins without grasping their purpose. Galen's followers held that blood was made in the liver and used up by the body. Harvey reasoned that the heart moved far too much blood for that to be true.
rte-harvey-de-motu-cordis.impact: Many physicians resisted the idea at first. Harvey could not see how arteries joined veins, and Marcello Malpighi found the capillaries with a microscope in 1661, after Harvey's death. The book became a model of experiment and measurement in physiology, though treatments such as bloodletting persisted.

rte-battle-of-white-mountain.why: In 1618 Protestant nobles threw two Habsburg officials from a window of Prague Castle in protest at threats to their religious freedoms. The Bohemian estates then deposed Ferdinand II and elected the Calvinist Frederick V of the Palatinate as king. Ferdinand won support from Bavaria, Spain and the Catholic League.
rte-battle-of-white-mountain.impact: Twenty-seven leaders of the revolt were executed in Prague in 1621. Rebel estates were confiscated and given to loyal Catholic families, Protestant worship was banned, and many thousands went into exile. The Bohemian crown became hereditary in the Habsburg family, and German gained ground in public life.

rte-giordano-bruno-burned.why: Bruno fled his Naples friary in 1576 when accused of heresy and spent years teaching in Geneva, Paris, London and Germany. He returned to Italy in 1591 to tutor a Venetian nobleman, Giovanni Mocenigo, who denounced him to the Inquisition. Venice then handed him over to Rome.
rte-giordano-bruno-burned.impact: His works were placed on the Index of Prohibited Books. In the nineteenth century Italian anticlericals adopted him as a martyr for free thought, and the statue was unveiled in 1889 over papal objections. Historians note that his condemnation rested mainly on theology, and much of the trial record is lost.

rte-napoleon-crowned-emperor.why: Napoleon had ruled as First Consul since his coup of 1799 and was made consul for life in 1802. Victories abroad, the Civil Code and peace with the Church made him popular. After a royalist assassination plot, the Senate proclaimed a hereditary empire, which a plebiscite approved.
rte-napoleon-crowned-emperor.impact: The title put Napoleon on a level with Europe's old dynasties and alarmed them. Within a year Austria and Russia were at war with him and were beaten at Austerlitz. In 1806 the Holy Roman Empire was dissolved. His empire lasted until his abdication in 1814.

rte-fort-sumter.why: Abraham Lincoln's election in 1860 on a platform opposing the spread of slavery led seven Southern states to secede and form the Confederacy. They seized most federal forts, but Sumter held out. When Lincoln announced he would send food to the garrison, Confederate leaders demanded its surrender.
rte-fort-sumter.impact: The attack united Northern opinion behind war. Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee and North Carolina joined the Confederacy, and Richmond became its capital. Both sides expected a short conflict. Instead the war lasted four years and killed at least 620,000 soldiers, with some recent estimates higher.

rte-emancipation-proclamation.why: Lincoln at first fought only to restore the Union, wary of losing the slaveholding border states. But enslaved people were fleeing to Union lines, abolitionists pressed him, and the war was going badly. He issued a preliminary warning after the Battle of Antietam in September 1862.
rte-emancipation-proclamation.impact: It did not apply to the border states or to some areas already under Union control, so freedom spread as the armies advanced. About 180,000 Black men served in the Union army. The proclamation also made it politically difficult for Britain or France to recognise the Confederacy.

rte-lincoln-assassinated.why: Booth, a well-known actor and Confederate sympathiser, had earlier plotted to kidnap Lincoln. After Richmond fell, and after hearing Lincoln speak in favour of votes for some Black men, he turned to murder. His accomplices were meant to kill the vice president and the secretary of state the same night.
rte-lincoln-assassinated.impact: Vice President Andrew Johnson, a Democrat from Tennessee, became president and proved lenient towards former Confederates. He clashed with Congress over the rights of freed people and was impeached in 1868, surviving by one vote. Four conspirators were hanged, among them Mary Surratt.

rte-slavery-abolition-act.why: Britain had banned the slave trade in 1807, but slavery itself continued. A mass movement of petitions and boycotts, in which women and nonconformist churches were prominent, kept up the pressure. A large uprising in Jamaica in 1831 and the reformed Parliament elected in 1832 tipped the balance.
rte-slavery-abolition-act.impact: The act came into force on 1 August 1834, and apprenticeship was ended early, in 1838, after protests. Territories run by the East India Company were excluded and dealt with later. The government loan raised to pay the compensation was not fully paid off until 2015.

rte-chile-independence.why: Napoleon's seizure of the Spanish throne in 1808 led Chileans to form their own junta in 1810. Royalist forces from Peru crushed this first government at Rancagua in 1814. In 1817 San Martín and O'Higgins led an army across the Andes from Argentina and won at Chacabuco.
rte-chile-independence.impact: O'Higgins ruled as Supreme Director until he was forced to resign in 1823. Chile built a navy, commanded by the British officer Thomas Cochrane, which carried San Martín's army north in 1820 to attack the royalist stronghold of Peru. Spain recognised Chilean independence in 1844.

rte-peterloo-massacre.why: The end of the Napoleonic Wars brought unemployment, and the Corn Laws kept bread dear. Fast-growing Manchester had no MPs of its own, while tiny boroughs elsewhere did. Reformers invited the orator Henry Hunt to speak, and local magistrates, fearing insurrection, ordered his arrest.
rte-peterloo-massacre.impact: The government backed the magistrates and passed the Six Acts, restricting meetings and radical newspapers. Hunt was jailed. Shelley wrote The Masque of Anarchy in response, though it was not published for years. Peterloo became a rallying memory for reformers, and Manchester gained MPs under the 1832 Reform Act.

rte-expedition-of-the-thousand.why: In 1859 Piedmont-Sardinia, with French help, had driven Austria from Lombardy, and the central Italian states then voted to join it. A revolt broke out in Sicily in April 1860 against Bourbon rule. Garibaldi, angered that his native Nice had been ceded to France, agreed to lead volunteers south.
rte-expedition-of-the-thousand.impact: Plebiscites joined the south to Piedmont, and the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in March 1861. Venetia followed in 1866 and Rome in 1870. Many southerners felt annexed, not liberated. Years of unrest known as brigandage followed, along with a lasting divide between north and south.

rte-russian-serfs-freed.why: Serfdom was widely seen as holding back Russia's economy and its conscript army, and peasant disturbances were growing. From 1857 Alexander set up committees of nobles and officials to work out terms. Their plan tried to free the peasants without ruining the landowners.
rte-russian-serfs-freed.impact: Land went to village communes, not individuals, and peasants often received less than they had farmed before. Disappointment led to unrest. Other reforms followed, including elected local councils, new courts and a reorganised army. The redemption payments were finally cancelled after the revolution of 1905.

rte-paris-commune.why: Paris had endured a four-month Prussian siege, with hunger and bombardment. Many Parisians felt betrayed by the armistice and by a newly elected, largely monarchist National Assembly. The assembly then ended the wartime freeze on rents and debts and stopped the pay of most National Guardsmen.
rte-paris-commune.impact: Estimates of those killed in the fighting and executions vary from about ten thousand to twenty thousand. Thousands more were imprisoned or deported to New Caledonia until an amnesty in 1880. Karl Marx and later Lenin treated the Commune as a model of workers' government.

rte-frankfurt-parliament.why: The German Confederation set up in 1815 was a loose league of some thirty-nine states dominated by Austria. Liberals wanted national unity and constitutional rights. After revolution broke out in Paris in February 1848, uprisings in Vienna and Berlin forced rulers to promise reforms and allow elections.
rte-frankfurt-parliament.impact: The delegates argued for months over whether Germany should include Austria, and they had no army of their own. Once the princes recovered their nerve the assembly was powerless. Unification came in 1871 under Bismarck, through war. Its list of basic rights influenced the constitutions of 1919 and 1949.

rte-decembrist-revolt.why: Officers who had marched to Paris in the wars against Napoleon came home ashamed of serfdom and autocracy, and formed secret societies. When Alexander I died suddenly, his brother Constantine had privately renounced the throne. The weeks of confusion before Nicholas took power gave them their chance.
rte-decembrist-revolt.impact: Nicholas I became deeply suspicious of reform. He created a political police, the Third Section, and tightened censorship throughout the thirty years of his reign. Several wives followed the exiles to Siberia, which added to the legend. The survivors were pardoned in 1856.

rte-belgian-independence.why: The mainly Catholic south resented rule by the Protestant King William I. Belgians had more people but no more seats in parliament, carried a share of the Dutch debt, and disliked the promotion of Dutch as an official language. The July Revolution in Paris in 1830 set an example.
rte-belgian-independence.impact: Dutch forces invaded in 1831 and withdrew when France intervened. The Netherlands accepted the separation in the Treaty of London of 1839. Belgium's liberal constitution of 1831 was widely admired. Germany's breach of Belgian neutrality in 1914 brought Britain into the First World War.

rte-maximilian-executed.why: After a civil war, Juárez's government suspended payments on foreign debts in 1861. France, Britain and Spain sent forces, but only France stayed, taking Mexico City in 1863. Mexican conservatives then invited Maximilian, younger brother of the Austrian emperor Franz Joseph, to take the throne.
rte-maximilian-executed.impact: European rulers had pleaded for his life, but Juárez wanted to deter further interventions. The failure damaged Napoleon III's standing at home and abroad. Maximilian's wife Charlotte suffered a mental collapse while seeking help in Europe. Édouard Manet painted the execution in works that could not be shown in France at the time.

rte-brazil-republic.why: Army officers felt undervalued after the Paraguayan War, and many had taken up republican and positivist ideas. The emperor had also quarrelled with the Church in the 1870s. Pedro II was ill and had no surviving sons, and many disliked the idea of his daughter Isabel succeeding him.
rte-brazil-republic.impact: There was little resistance or bloodshed. A constitution of 1891 created a federal republic modelled partly on the United States, and Church and state were separated. Politics came to be dominated by the coffee and cattle elites of São Paulo and Minas Gerais until a coup in 1930.

rte-roentgen-x-rays.why: Physicists across Europe were studying cathode rays, the glowing beams produced when electricity passes through a tube with most of the air removed. Röntgen had covered his tube in black card to block its light, so the glow on a screen some distance away had to come from something new.
rte-roentgen-x-rays.impact: Röntgen refused to patent the discovery, so its use spread freely. It led Henri Becquerel to find radioactivity in 1896. The dangers of exposure were learned slowly, through burns and cancers among early workers. X-ray diffraction later revealed the structure of crystals and of DNA.

rte-golden-spike.why: The California Gold Rush and the acquisition of the west coast made a rail link urgent. With Southern members absent, Congress passed the Pacific Railway Act in 1862, offering land grants and loans. Chinese labourers built much of the Central Pacific and Irish immigrants much of the Union Pacific.
rte-golden-spike.impact: The line opened the West to settlers and tied California's economy to the East. It was a disaster for the Plains peoples, bringing hunters who destroyed the bison herds and troops who forced nations onto reservations. Railway timetables later led to standard time zones in 1883.

rte-edison-phonograph.why: Edison was working on ways to record telegraph messages and improve the telephone. He noticed that a stylus attached to a vibrating diaphragm could indent moving paper or foil. In the 1850s the Frenchman Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville had traced sound waves on paper, but could not play them back.
rte-edison-phonograph.impact: Tinfoil wore out after a few plays, and Edison set the machine aside to work on electric light. Rivals developed wax cylinders in the 1880s, and Emile Berliner introduced the flat disc gramophone. Edison at first expected the main use to be office dictation, not music.

rte-brooklyn-bridge.why: Brooklyn was a separate and fast-growing city whose workers relied on ferries that ice and fog could stop. John Roebling had already built wire suspension bridges at Niagara and Cincinnati. Washington Roebling was disabled by decompression sickness from the underwater caissons, so Emily relayed his instructions to the site.
rte-brooklyn-bridge.impact: The bridge encouraged Brooklyn's growth and its merger into Greater New York in 1898. Its use of steel wire and its tall stone towers influenced later long-span bridges. It carried trains and trams for decades and remains in daily use by cars, cyclists and pedestrians.

rte-nobel-dynamite.why: Nitroglycerine, first made by Ascanio Sobrero in 1847, was powerful but could explode from a knock. A blast at the Nobel family works in Stockholm in 1864 killed Alfred's younger brother Emil and several others. Nobel then looked for a way to make it stable enough to transport.
rte-nobel-dynamite.impact: It was used on projects such as the Gotthard rail tunnel and later the Panama Canal, and also in war and in bombings by revolutionaries. Nobel went on to invent blasting gelatine and a smokeless powder. His will of 1895 set up the prizes, first awarded in 1901.

rte-stockton-darlington-railway.why: Colliery owners around Darlington, led by the Quaker merchant Edward Pease, needed a cheaper way to move coal than packhorses and carts. They first planned a horse-drawn line. Stephenson, who had built engines for Killingworth colliery, persuaded Pease that steam locomotives could do the work.
rte-stockton-darlington-railway.impact: Coal prices at Stockton fell sharply, and the new port of Middlesbrough grew up where the line was extended. Passengers were at first carried in horse-drawn coaches. The track gauge Stephenson used, later widened by half an inch, became the standard on most of the world's railways.

rte-faraday-induction.why: In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted had shown that an electric current deflects a compass needle. Faraday, a blacksmith's son who began as a bookbinder's apprentice and became assistant to Humphry Davy, spent years asking whether the reverse was possible, with magnetism producing electricity.
rte-faraday-induction.impact: Joseph Henry found the same effect independently in the United States. Faraday's idea of lines of force was later put into mathematical form by James Clerk Maxwell, whose equations predicted electromagnetic waves. Practical generators developed over the following decades made public electricity supply possible by the 1880s.

rte-ss-great-britain.why: Brunel's wooden paddle steamer Great Western had shown in 1838 that a regular Atlantic steam service could work. For its successor he chose iron, which allowed a much larger hull than timber. After seeing the experimental ship Archimedes, he changed the design from paddle wheels to a propeller.
rte-ss-great-britain.impact: The ship crossed to New York in 1845. It ran aground in Ireland in 1846, and the cost of salvage ruined its owners. It later carried thousands of emigrants to Australia, then ended as a storage hulk in the Falkland Islands before being towed home in 1970.

rte-mendeleev-periodic-table.why: More than sixty elements were known, and chemists had noticed family likenesses among them. The Karlsruhe Congress of 1860 helped chemists agree on atomic weights. Mendeleev was writing a textbook and needed a clear way to order the elements. Lothar Meyer in Germany reached a similar scheme at about the same time.
rte-mendeleev-periodic-table.impact: The noble gases, found in the 1890s, fitted in as a new group. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed that the true ordering principle is atomic number, not weight, which resolved several anomalies. Element 101 is named mendelevium. Mendeleev himself never won a Nobel Prize.

rte-pasteur-rabies-vaccine.why: Pasteur had already made vaccines for chicken cholera and anthrax by weakening the microbes that cause them. For rabies he and Émile Roux used dried spinal cord from infected rabbits, tested on dogs. The boy's mother brought him from Alsace two days after he was bitten.
rte-pasteur-rabies-vaccine.impact: A second patient, a shepherd boy named Jean-Baptiste Jupille, was treated successfully that autumn, and people came from across Europe and beyond. The case showed that vaccination could work after exposure. Historians reading Pasteur's notebooks have since questioned how thoroughly the method had been tested beforehand.

rte-fulton-steamboat.why: John Fitch and others had run steamboats earlier but failed to make them pay. Fulton, an American artist turned engineer, had tested a steamboat on the Seine in 1803. His partner Robert Livingston held a monopoly on steam navigation in New York waters, and the engine came from Boulton and Watt in England.
rte-fulton-steamboat.impact: By 1811 a steamboat was heading down the Ohio and Mississippi, and upstream travel transformed trade in the interior. The Livingston and Fulton monopoly was struck down by the Supreme Court in Gibbons v. Ogden in 1824, a ruling that confirmed federal power over commerce between states.

rte-ether-day.why: Surgery was agonising and had to be done in minutes. Ether and nitrous oxide were known mainly as party amusements. The dentist Horace Wells had tried to demonstrate nitrous oxide in Boston in 1845, and it failed. Morton, his former partner, tested ether on the advice of the chemist Charles Jackson.
rte-ether-day.impact: Morton, Jackson and Wells quarrelled bitterly over credit, as did supporters of Crawford Long, a Georgia doctor who had used ether in 1842 without publishing. Chloroform followed in 1847. Surgeons could now work slowly, though deaths from infection stayed high until antiseptic methods arrived.

rte-broad-street-pump.why: Cholera had reached Britain in 1831 and returned in waves. London's cesspools and sewers leaked into wells and the Thames. Snow, a pioneer of anaesthesia, had argued since 1849 that the disease was swallowed in water. The Soho outbreak killed more than 500 people within about ten days.
rte-broad-street-pump.impact: The outbreak was already fading when the handle came off, and officials still rejected Snow's theory. A local clergyman, Henry Whitehead, later helped trace the source to a nearby cesspool. Snow died in 1858. Joseph Bazalgette's great London sewer system was built in the years that followed.

rte-transatlantic-telegraph-cable.why: Telegraph lines covered much of Europe and North America by the 1850s, but news between them took about ten days by ship. The American businessman Cyrus Field raised money on both sides of the ocean. Attempts in 1857 and earlier in 1858 failed when the cable snapped during laying.
rte-transatlantic-telegraph-cable.impact: The signals were very weak, and an attempt to force them through with high voltage ruined the insulation. A British inquiry, with advice from William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, led to better cable design. After 1866 market prices and news crossed the ocean in minutes.

rte-koch-tuberculosis.why: Koch, a former country doctor, had shown in 1876 that a specific bacterium causes anthrax. He then developed staining methods and solid culture media for growing pure colonies. The tuberculosis bacillus was hard to see and grew slowly, and many doctors thought the disease was inherited.
rte-koch-tuberculosis.impact: Koch's announcement of a cure, tuberculin, in 1890 proved a failure, though the substance became a diagnostic test. He received the Nobel Prize in 1905. The BCG vaccine followed in 1921 and effective antibiotics in the 1940s. Tuberculosis still kills more than a million people a year.
